headline_en: Promised Malaysia, taken around the sea for four days, then dumped on Cox's Bazar beach by a broker ring that fled
summary_en: 72 people, mostly Rohingya, boarded a trawler off Teknaf on 16 November 2026 to be taken illegally by sea to Malaysia. After four days at sea and a quarrel between the crew and the brokers, the trawler landed them at Laboni Point, Cox's Bazar beach, late on Friday 20 November and the crew and brokers fled. Police rescued 28 people; the rest ran away. A case against unnamed brokers was being prepared.

facts.statement: On Monday 16 November 2026 (evening), 72 people were taken in several small fishing boats from Mithapanir Chhara boat landing (Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar) to the deep sea and put on a large wooden trawler waiting there, which set off that night saying it was going to Malaysia.
facts.source_in_article: rescued passengers speaking to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: People trying to go illegally by sea to Malaysia from Teknaf in November 2026 had each paid the broker ring BDT 10,000 to 15,000.

Because the Bay of Bengal turned rough under the influence of a cyclone, the Malaysia-bound trawler stayed near the coast close to St Martin's Island; the brokers kept the passengers at sea for four days and nobody was taken to Malaysia.

After a dispute between the trawler's crew and the brokers on Thursday night (19 November 2026) over taking the passengers to Malaysia, the crew brought the trawler to Cox's Bazar beach on Friday night 20 November, told the passengers to get down into the water and run, and the crew and brokers fled leaving the trawler on the beach.
facts.source_in_article: rescued passengers; OC Sheikh Mohammad Ali

facts.statement: At about 11:30 pm on Friday 20 November 2026 the trawler reached Laboni Point on Cox's Bazar beach; passengers jumped into waist-deep water, some hid in the nearby tamarisk (jhau) grove and groups fled towards the town. Tourist Police and district police rescued 28 people: 25 men, 2 women and 1 child; the rest of the 72 got away.
facts.source_in_article: eyewitnesses; OC Sheikh Mohammad Ali, Cox's Bazar Sadar Model Thana

facts.statement: Most of the 28 people rescued at Cox's Bazar beach after the failed sea trip to Malaysia were Rohingya; the others were residents of Teknaf (Cox's Bazar), Naikhongchhari (Bandarban) and other districts of Bangladesh.
Police said the 28 rescued people were being identified; after that the Rohingya would be handed to the refugee camps and the Bangladeshis to their families.

The trawler used for the trafficking attempt was seized and kept in Coast Guard custody; police were trying to identify and arrest the brokers who fled and were preparing a case at Cox's Bazar Sadar Model Thana against several unnamed brokers.

Rescued passenger Md. Ilias said he and 16 others were put on one small boat at Mithapanir Chhara boat landing on Teknaf beach on the evening of 16 November 2026 and transferred in the deep sea to a larger trawler that already had more than 40 men and women on board; the trawler left that night with 72 passengers, and it carried 17 crew and brokers.

headline_en: Seven Habiganj youths were going from Libya to Greece; six missing after boat sinks
summary_en: Seven young men from Madhabpur and Lakhai upazilas of Habiganj left Libya for Greece on 31 October 2026 in an inflatable rubber boat arranged by brokers; the boat sprang a leak and sank in the Mediterranean. Only Masum Mia survived, reaching Greece after two days adrift; six are missing. Families paid the brokers BDT 12 to 15 lakh each and cannot reach the Dhaka-based brokers. The UNO said families must apply formally to the ministry so the foreign ministry and embassy can search.

facts.statement: On 31 October 2026 seven young men from Madhabpur and Lakhai upazilas of Habiganj set off through brokers from Libya for Greece in an air-inflated rubber boat carrying about fifty passengers.

In the middle of the Mediterranean the inflatable boat from Libya to Greece developed a hole, water came in quickly and the boat sank, throwing all passengers into the sea; six of the seven Habiganj men are missing and more than 15 days later their families had no news.
facts.source_in_article: Maraj Mia, father of survivor Masum Mia, quoting his son; families

facts.statement: Survivor Masum Mia of Puraikola village, Madhabpur, Habiganj stayed afloat in the waves, came ashore unconscious two days later and finally reached Greece with the help of local residents; he phoned his family about three days before 17 November 2026 and told them of the sinking.
facts.source_in_article: Maraj Mia, father of Masum Mia

facts.statement: Families of the missing Habiganj men said the broker ring took BDT 12 lakh to 15 lakh from each of them for delivery to Greece; some sold land and some borrowed at high interest to raise the money.
After learning of the sinking the families tried to contact the brokers, who are based in Dhaka, but could not reach them; one father said the families do not even know the brokers' address.
facts.source_in_article: relatives; Habib Mia, father of Naim Mia

facts.statement: Madhabpur UNO Mehedi Hasan said that to trace the missing young men the affected families must apply through due process to the relevant government ministry; once a formal application is received, a search at international level can be arranged through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the embassy.
facts.source_in_article: Mehedi Hasan, Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Madhabpur

facts.statement: The six missing are Pavel Mia and Ataur Mia of Puraikola village, Alamgir Mia of Kaura village, Naim Mia of Baghasura village and Sagar Mia of Chhatiain union (all Madhabpur upazila), and Abul Mia of Lakhai upazila, Habiganj; they are aged 25 to 30.

headline_en: 200 years since the abolition of slavery
summary_en: A reprint (online on 11 November 2026) of a historical essay first printed in Prothom Alo on 4 January 2008 about the history and abolition of slavery. Almost all of it is world history; a closing section on modern slavery gives undated, pre-2008 figures on human trafficking, including trafficking of women and children from Bangladesh to India and Pakistan. Nothing in it is current guidance for migrant workers.

facts.date: as of the essay's first publication on 4 January 2008 (no period given)
facts.statement: A 2008 essay reprinted in 2026 states that human trafficking takes place at 21 locations in the southern and south-western districts of Bangladesh, and that 200 to 400 women and children are trafficked to Pakistan each month and 10,000 to 16,000 to India each year; relatives, neighbours and brokers work together with foreign criminal rings. No source is given for these figures.

The 2008 essay cites the International Labour Organization as estimating that 12.3 million people live in slavery-like conditions (forced labour, bonded labour, forced child labour, sexual slavery), and says 1 to 2 million people are sold across international borders each year, mostly women and a significant share children; trafficking occurs from about 127 countries and victims are used in about 137 countries, earning about USD 9.5 billion a year.
facts.source_in_article: essay author citing ILO for the 12.3 million figure

facts.statement: The 2008 essay says slavery has reappeared in the modern age through human trafficking: desperate poor migrants often have to work in slavery-like conditions and a large network traffics people to Western Europe and America wherever cheap labour is needed.
The 2008 essay says Bangladesh's Penal Code contains anti-slavery provisions and that an article of the Constitution prohibits all forms of forced labour.

The essay describes the European Court of Human Rights case Siliadin v. France (2005): a Togolese girl brought to France in 1994 at age 15 and a half worked as an unpaid domestic from 7:30 am to 10:30 pm; the court held she was subjected to forced labour (not slavery in the literal sense) and that France failed in its duty, awarding EUR 26,209.69 for legal costs and no compensation because she had not asked for it.

headline_en: Remittances below USD 3 billion for five straight months; dollar price rising
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show remittances of USD 2.84 billion in October 2026, the fifth month in a row under USD 3 billion, though 12 percent above October 2025. FY2025-26 remittances hit a record USD 35.59 billion. The article also gives interbank, bank cash and kerb-market dollar rates as of Thursday 29 October 2026, including what banks pay returnees for cash dollars.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh were USD 284 crore (2.84 billion) in October 2026, the fifth consecutive month below USD 300 crore; the last month above USD 300 crore was May 2026.
Monthly remittances in FY2026-27 were USD 285 crore 87 lakh in July 2026, USD 296 crore 66 lakh in August 2026 and USD 276 crore 60 lakh in September 2026.
October 2026 remittances were 12 percent higher than October 2025, when USD 256 crore came in.
Expatriates sent a record total of USD 3,559 crore (35.59 billion) in FY2025-26; in six of that year's twelve months remittances exceeded USD 300 crore.
In FY2024-25 remittances through banks grew about 27 percent and exceeded USD 30 billion for the first time, after a jump following the political changeover two years before November 2026.

People in the sector said remittance flow had not fallen much because of the ease of sending money through banking channels and a stable official dollar rate, and that the war-related unrest in Middle East countries had not had a big effect.
Banks bought dollars from each other at a maximum of BDT 123.60 on 19 October 2026, rising to BDT 123.99 on Thursday 29 October 2026; the price rose by 5 to 20 paisa every day in that period.

On Thursday 29 October 2026 City Bank bought cash dollars from people returning from abroad at BDT 124.75 and sold at BDT 126; BRAC Bank bought returnees' dollars at BDT 125.50 and sold at BDT 126.50; United Commercial Bank (UCB) bought at BDT 125 and sold at BDT 126.25; Agrani Bank bought cash dollars at BDT 123 and sold at BDT 124.
facts.source_in_article: reporter's review of banks' declared rates

facts.statement: On Thursday 29 October 2026 the open market and money changers in Motijheel, Dhaka sold dollars at BDT 128.50 and money changers bought dollars from customers at up to BDT 128, higher than bank rates (up to BDT 126.50).

headline_en: Medical tests for workers wishing to go to Malaysia start from 31 October
summary_en: In a directive issued on Wednesday 28 October 2026, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment said medical tests for workers going to Malaysia begin on 31 October 2026 at approved medical centres only; tests done earlier will not be accepted or processed for immigration clearance. It warned that brokers and dishonest agencies were trying to take passports and money for unauthorised tests and set out penalties for centres and agencies that disobey.

facts.statement: Medical tests for workers wishing to go to Malaysia for work start on 31 October 2026; no medical test may be done before that date, and any test done before 31 October will not be accepted and will not be processed for immigration clearance.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment directive of 28 October 2026

facts.statement: The Malaysia medical tests are to be done at approved medical centres; the ministry said the list of approved medical centres would be published on its website very soon and asked workers to keep checking the ministry website for the listed centres.

No medical centre or recruiting agency may carry out or arrange workers' medical tests for Malaysia without the ministry's instruction and approval; a medical centre that fails to comply with government instructions will be dropped from the list.
The ministry said it had noticed that some brokers and dishonest agencies were trying to take passports and money from workers by offering to arrange Malaysia medical tests without permission.
The ministry asked workers not to respond to offers of unauthorised medical tests and not to give their passport or money to anyone without first confirming the approval.
Until further notice, agencies applying for BMET clearance (for Malaysia) must submit the relevant papers for testing at an approved medical centre.

The ministry said action under existing laws and rules would be taken against medical centres and recruiting agencies that defy the directive: the centre's operations may be shut, the recruiting agency's overseas recruitment activities suspended and the ministry's approval cancelled.
Workers who know of illegal or unapproved medical tests are asked to inform the ministry with the date and place of the incident, the name of the person or organisation involved, and evidence.

headline_en: Children of expatriate workers to get education scholarships; application details
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board invited online applications (25 October to 24 November 2026) for scholarships for meritorious children of expatriate workers who passed SSC 2026, HSC 2025 or Diploma-in-Engineering 2025. The article sets out eligibility, minimum GPAs (lower for children of workers who died abroad), required documents, scholarship duration, and the call-centre numbers.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board (under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment) invited applications for education scholarships for meritorious children of expatriate workers; online applications open on 25 October 2026 and close on 24 November 2026.

To be eligible for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship the student's father or mother must have taken BMET emigration clearance or be a member of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board; at most two children of one expatriate worker can apply.

Eligible groups: students who passed SSC or equivalent in 2026 and are studying in class 11 or equivalent or the first semester/year of Diploma-in-Engineering; students who passed HSC or equivalent in 2025 and are in the first semester/year at a university or medical college; and students who passed Diploma-in-Engineering in 2025 under the Bangladesh Technical Education Board and are in the first semester/year of BSc in Engineering at a university.

Minimum GPA for SSC 2026: science group 5.00 in the general case and 4.00 for children of workers who died abroad; humanities and business studies 4.75 in the general case and 4.00 for children of deceased workers.

Minimum GPA for HSC 2025: science group 4.80, humanities and business studies 4.50; for children of workers who died abroad the minimum is 4.00 for both groups. For Diploma-in-Engineering 2025: 3.25 in the general case and 3.00 for children of workers who died abroad.

Documents to submit with the scholarship application: copy of the expatriate worker's passport, BMET emigration clearance or proof of Wage Earners' Welfare Board membership, a certificate from the educational institution (which must carry the mobile number of the head of the institution), the student's bank account statement, photo, signature, and a copy of birth registration or national ID.
For children of workers who died abroad, a no-objection certificate (NOC) issued by the Bangladesh mission abroad must be submitted with the scholarship application.
The student must have an account in his or her own name at any scheduled bank; agent banking accounts are not accepted.

Scholarship duration: two years (class 11 to 12) for SSC passers; up to four years for Diploma-in-Engineering students; for HSC passers three years for degree (pass) courses and four years at honours/bachelor level; five years for MBBS, BDS, DVM, B.Arch and other applicable courses; four years at BSc-in-Engineering level for Diploma-in-Engineering passers.
Applications must be made online through the website; applications submitted in person or by post will not be accepted. (The article does not print the website address.)

An application may be cancelled if the name in the expatriate worker's passport does not match the father's or mother's name on the student's certificate; incomplete applications and those with wrong information are also treated as cancelled.
For scholarship information contact the Probashi call centre: 16135 (from inside Bangladesh, toll free) or +8809610203030 (from abroad).

headline_en: Bangladesh has not fully met minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking
summary_en: The US State Department's 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, published Thursday 8 October 2026, keeps Bangladesh on Tier 2: it does not fully meet the minimum standards but is making significant efforts. The report credits a new 2026 ordinance, more investigations and stronger migrant-worker protection, but notes fewer convictions, fewer victims identified, weak protection for returnee migrant workers and Rohingya, and that workers still pay recruitment fees themselves.

facts.statement: The US State Department's 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, published on 8 October 2026, keeps Bangladesh on Tier 2 as before: the government has not fully met the minimum standards for eliminating trafficking but is making significant efforts. India, Pakistan, Bhutan and Sri Lanka are on the same tier.
The TIP Report 2026 says the Bangladesh government passed the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking and Migrant Smuggling Ordinance, 2026 to strengthen the legal framework.

According to the TIP Report 2026, Bangladesh increased trafficking investigations and prosecutions, updated guidelines for detecting trafficking offences and identifying victims, piloted a digital system to speed help to victims and improve coordination between agencies, and strengthened protection of migrant workers.

The TIP Report 2026 says fewer traffickers were convicted than before, fewer victims were identified, the government did not take enough steps against trafficking inside the country, and the crime remains widespread.
The TIP Report 2026 says protection and rehabilitation of victims is inadequate, with the gap greatest for Rohingya refugees and migrant workers who have returned to Bangladesh.

The TIP Report 2026 says the Bangladesh government has not ended the system under which migrant workers pay recruitment fees out of their own pockets; as a result many workers fall into debt, which raises their risk of becoming trafficking victims.

Tier definitions as explained: Tier 1 countries meet the minimum standards set in US law; Tier 2 countries do not fully meet them but are making significant efforts (with a Tier 2 Watch List within it); Tier 3 countries neither meet the standards nor make significant efforts.

headline_en: Why so many questions at immigration whenever a woman travels abroad alone
summary_en: Three unmarried adult women from Dinajpur, Thakurgaon and Naogaon were stopped by immigration police at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 8 August 2026 on their way to Nepal despite valid papers; on 29 September 2026 the High Court issued a rule asking why this should not be declared without lawful authority. Police sources say Nepal is being used as a trafficking route and its on-arrival visa means extra document checks at the airport. Other women, including the reporter, describe being questioned at Dhaka immigration about husbands, guardians and travel purpose.

facts.statement: According to their writ petition, three adult unmarried women from Dinajpur, Thakurgaon and Naogaon went to Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport at 9 am on 8 August 2026 for a 10:05 am flight to Nepal with tickets and the necessary travel papers, but the officer-in-charge of immigration police, Abdullah, refused to let them travel; they say they were given no written notice or legal reason and there was no court ban or other legal bar on their travel.

On Tuesday 29 September 2026, after a preliminary hearing on the three women's writ, the High Court issued a rule asking why stopping them from travelling abroad should not be declared to be without lawful authority, and why the authorities should not be directed to frame and issue guidelines so that adult women citizens are not stopped from lawful foreign travel merely for being unmarried, travelling without a guardian or on similar gender-based grounds.

Lawyer Ishrat Hasan, who argued the writ, said the immigration officer's conduct raises questions under Articles 27 and 28 (equality and non-discrimination on grounds of sex), 31 and 32 (protection of law and personal liberty) and 36 (freedom of movement) of the Constitution; she said a legal notice had been sent to the Additional Inspector General of Police and got no reply.

A person who answered the official mobile of the Special Superintendent of Police (Immigration Operations), Special Branch, without identifying himself, asked why the three women could not show a hotel booking or say which seminar they were going to; police officers speaking anonymously claimed the women said they were going to a seminar but could not show an invitation letter.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed Special Branch immigration official; unnamed police officers

facts.statement: Police officers speaking anonymously said the Bangladesh government has been warned that Nepal is being used as a route for human trafficking from Bangladesh; because Nepal offers a visa on arrival, special attention is being paid to checking documents at the airport, and a passenger is stopped if any document looks suspicious.
Assistant Inspector General A H M Shahadat Hossain of the Police Headquarters media wing said the matter of the three women is sub judice and declined to comment.
facts.source_in_article: A H M Shahadat Hossain, AIG (media), Police Headquarters

facts.statement: Gender analyst Sabina Parvin said that in November 2025, when her family was flying to Nepal for a family event, an immigration officer stopped a 52-year-old woman travelling with them because she was not a family member; she was taken to a more senior officer and got her passport back only after a long argument, the officers reasoning that a woman travelling alone could be a trafficking victim.
facts.source_in_article: Sabina Parvin, gender analyst (Facebook post and interview)

facts.statement: Rights activist Ferdous Ara Rumee said that a few years ago five women from five NGOs were flying to Nepal for a seven-day workshop, all with invitation letters; four passed immigration but one was held, asked whether her husband knew she was going, made to give her husband's phone number, and the immigration officer phoned the husband from his own phone to confirm.
facts.source_in_article: Ferdous Ara Rumee, spokesperson of Network for People's Action (NPA)

facts.statement: The reporter (a woman journalist) says that about 14 years ago, flying alone at dawn to Abu Dhabi on a prize ticket, a Dhaka immigration officer repeatedly questioned her reason for travel despite her passport showing her profession, marital status and earlier travel stamps, and insisted she phone her relative in Abu Dhabi (about 3 am there) so he could speak to the relative before letting her go.
Ferdous Ara Rumee said immigration officers are more suspicious when they hear a woman is travelling alone to countries such as Thailand or Nepal.

Dhaka University professor Tania Haque said the authorities should disclose in what context the three women were not allowed to go, that without evidence of criminal activity there is no justification for stopping three adult women on suspicion alone, and that anyone found negligent or abusing power should be held accountable.
facts.source_in_article: Tania Haque, professor, Women and Gender Studies, Dhaka University

headline_en: Preparations for Prime Minister's visits to three countries in the next two months
summary_en: Diplomatic sources told Prothom Alo on 26 September 2026 that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is preparing to visit Japan in the last week of October, Turkey for the COP31 leaders' summit in November, and Saudi Arabia in the second half of November 2026. For migration, the article notes the Japan visit may review progress on manpower export against a target of 100,000 skilled workers in five years set in May 2025, and that more than 2.8 million Bangladeshi workers are in Saudi Arabia.

facts.statement: During then Chief Adviser Professor Muhammad Yunus's visit to Tokyo in May 2025, a target was set of sending 100,000 skilled Bangladeshi workers to Japan in five years; seven memorandums of understanding on investment, energy and technology were signed.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is due to visit Tokyo for three to four days in the last week of October 2026 at the invitation of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi; review of progress on manpower export may be among the priorities, along with investment and a business conference.
facts.source_in_article: diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Tokyo

facts.statement: More than 28 lakh (2.8 million) Bangladeshi workers are currently employed in Saudi Arabia, making it Bangladesh's largest labour market.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman may visit Riyadh in the second half of November 2026 at the invitation of Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman; expected topics are bilateral relations, energy imports, investment agreements, regional and international issues and continued Saudi support on the Rohingya question. Labour issues are not listed among the expected topics.

Saudi Arabia has in recent years expressed interest in taking its relationship with Bangladesh beyond traditional manpower export; in August 2026 Saudi deputy foreign minister Waleed El-Khereiji, at a meeting in Dhaka, expressed interest in investing in fisheries, food, energy, renewable energy, IT and artificial intelligence.

key_quote_bn: বর্তমানে ২৮ লাখের বেশি বাংলাদেশি শ্রমিক সৌদি আরবে কর্মরত, যা দেশটিকে বাংলাদেশের বৃহত্তম শ্রমবাজারে পরিণত করেছে।

headline_en: PM mourns deaths of 16 Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia, orders bodies brought home quickly
summary_en: Sixteen Bangladeshis died in a fire at a sofa factory in Riyadh on Monday 10 August 2026. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman expressed condolences, promised the families all necessary help, and directed the foreign ministry, the expatriates' welfare ministry and the Riyadh embassy to coordinate to bring the bodies home as fast as possible.

facts.statement: On Monday 10 August 2026 a fire at a sofa-making factory in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia killed 16 Bangladeshis.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman directed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment and the Bangladesh Embassy in Riyadh to act in coordination to bring the bodies of the 16 fire victims home in the shortest possible time, with the Prime Minister's Office to give all necessary cooperation; he assured the families of all necessary help. No amounts or dates are given.
facts.source_in_article: Saleh Shibli, Prime Minister's press secretary

key_quote_bn: গতকাল সোমবার রিয়াদে একটি সোফা তৈরির কারখানায় ভয়াবহ আগুনে ১৬ জন বাংলাদেশি প্রাণ হারান।

headline_en: Remittances below USD 3 billion for two straight months; why
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank figures released on 2 August 2026 show remittances of about USD 2.86 billion in July 2026 after USD 2.82 billion in June, following six straight months above USD 3 billion. Bankers link the dip to Bangladesh Bank tightening oversight after banks bought remittance dollars at higher prices; the Middle East crisis is also mentioned. Islami Bank leads remittance collection, followed by Bangladesh Krishi Bank.

facts.statement: Remittances were about USD 286 crore in July 2026 (stated precisely as USD 285 crore 90 lakh) and USD 282 crore in June 2026, after six consecutive months above USD 300 crore.
July 2026 remittances of USD 285 crore 90 lakh were 15.4 percent higher than the USD 247 crore 78 lakh of the same month a year earlier.

Monthly remittances: December 2025 USD 322 crore; January 2026 USD 317 crore; February 2026 USD 302 crore; March 2026 about USD 375 crore; April 2026 USD 312 crore 70 lakh; May 2026 USD 342 crore 50 lakh 30 thousand.
Islami Bank is at the top in collecting remittances, followed by Bangladesh Krishi Bank.

After banks bought remittance dollars at higher prices, Bangladesh Bank increased its monitoring, and remittance inflow then fell somewhat; bank officials said this may be why the flow dropped. The article also says the dollar price for remittances rose because of the Middle East crisis.
Bankers noted that remittances stayed above USD 3 billion for six months even though manpower export did not increase.

key_quote_bn: প্রবাসী আয় সংগ্রহে শীর্ষে রয়েছে ইসলামী ব্যাংক।

headline_en: Relief on remittances and reserves, worry over exports
summary_en: At the start of FY2026-27 the article reports record remittances of about USD 35 billion in the previous twelve months despite the Middle East crisis, lifting usable reserves to about USD 32 billion, while goods exports fell. A former Bangladesh Bank chief economist attributes the rise to less hundi, a narrower gap between legal and illegal dollar rates and easier legal sending and receiving.

facts.statement: Up to 27 June of FY2025-26, remittances of USD 35.20 billion (USD 3,520 crore) came to Bangladesh, the highest ever and 16 percent more than the previous fiscal year; from December 2025 to May 2026 every month brought USD 3 billion.
In FY2024-25 remittances through banks grew about 27 percent and crossed USD 30 billion for the first time, after a jump following the political changeover two years before mid-2026.

Former Bangladesh Bank chief economist Mustafa K Mujeri said a main reason remittances rose is that less money comes through hundi; the gap between the dollar price in legal and illegal channels has narrowed and sending and receiving money legally has become easier. He said new markets must be found and skilled workers sent to keep the trend.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafa K Mujeri, former chief economist, Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: Bankers, businesspeople and economists said remittance growth would have more room if the war between Iran and the United States-Israel stops completely, and that if the Middle East crisis is not resolved all calculations would change.

Gross reserves rose from USD 31.77 billion on 30 June 2025 (USD 26.74 billion under IMF BPM6) to USD 36.08 billion in June 2026 (USD 31.53 billion under BPM6), helped by remittance growth; usable reserves are about USD 32 billion.

key_quote_bn: প্রবাসী আয় বাড়ার অন্যতম প্রধান কারণ হুন্ডিতে অর্থ আসা কমে যাওয়া।

headline_en: Extra subsidy of BDT 42,600 crore needed for oil, gas, power and fertiliser: Finance Minister in parliament
summary_en: Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury told parliament on Tuesday 9 June 2026 that conflict in Iran and the Middle East may require about BDT 42,600 crore in extra subsidies for oil, gas, power and fertiliser in FY2025-26. The only migration content is his statement that the unrest is visibly affecting remittances and overseas employment, that prolonged instability is a risk to both, and that the government is looking for alternative labour markets.

facts.statement: Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury told parliament on 9 June 2026 that the effects of the recent unrest in Iran and the Middle East are so far most visible in fuel, fertiliser, import and transport costs, inflation, foreign-exchange management, remittances and overseas employment, and that since the Middle East is an important destination for Bangladeshi migrant workers, prolonged instability could put overseas employment and remittance flow at risk.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, in parliament

facts.statement: The Finance Minister said the government is taking steps including searching for alternative labour markets in response to the Middle East situation; no markets are named.
facts.source_in_article: Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury, in parliament

key_quote_bn: মধ্যপ্রাচ্য বাংলাদেশের প্রবাসী কর্মীদের গুরুত্বপূর্ণ গন্তব্য হওয়ায় দীর্ঘস্থায়ী অস্থিরতা বৈদেশিক কর্মসংস্থান ও প্রবাসী আয়প্রবাহের ক্ষেত্রেও ঝুঁকি তৈরি করতে পারে।

headline_en: Two Bangladeshis killed in Israeli drone strike in Lebanon
summary_en: Two Bangladeshi workers from Satkhira were killed when an Israeli drone struck a residence in the Zebdin area of Nabatieh, southern Lebanon, around noon local time on Monday 11 May 2026. The Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut confirmed the deaths and said the bodies are at Nabih Berri Hospital in Nabatieh. A Bangladeshi woman worker, Dipali Begum, was killed in an Israeli air strike in Beirut on 8 April 2026.

facts.statement: On Monday (11 May 2026) at about 12 noon local time an Israeli drone strike on a residence in the Zebdin area of Nabatieh, southern Lebanon killed two Bangladeshi workers: Shafiqul Islam, son of Afsar Ali of Bhaluka Chandpur village, Satkhira Sadar upazila, and Md. Nahidul Islam, son of Md. Abdul Kader of Kadakati village, Ashashuni upazila, Satkhira.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut said the two men's bodies were being kept at Nabih Berri Hospital in Nabatieh; the article says nothing about repatriation or compensation.
On 8 April 2026 Bangladeshi woman worker Dipali Begum was killed in an Israeli air strike in Beirut.

headline_en: 8,000 would-be migrants dead or missing in one year: IOM
summary_en: An IOM report published on Tuesday 21 April 2026 says 7,904 people were reported dead or missing on migration routes in 2025, against 9,197 in 2024, with sea routes to Europe the deadliest. The lower figure is largely because about 1,500 suspected deaths could not be verified after aid cuts. IOM says flows from Bangladesh have risen and Bangladeshis have emerged as the largest group of migrants arriving in Europe.

facts.statement: IOM reported that 7,904 people were recorded dead or missing on migration routes in 2025, compared with 9,197 in 2024, which the article calls the highest number of migrant deaths in any single year.
IOM said a major reason the 2025 figure was lower than the year before is that, because of reduced aid, about 1,500 suspected deaths could not be independently verified.

More than 4 in every 10 deaths or disappearances occurred on sea routes towards Europe, the deadliest routes; many victims were lost in 'invisible shipwrecks' in which whole boats full of migrants sank or vanished and were never found.
Since 2014 the number of migrants killed on these routes has exceeded 82,000, directly affecting about 340,000 families.

IOM said that although arrivals of migrants in Europe fell overall, routes and source countries changed: against a background of political and policy shifts the flow from Bangladesh increased and Bangladeshis emerged as the largest group of would-be migrants in Europe, while the flow from Syria decreased.
IOM Director General Amy Pope said routes may be changing because of conflicts, climate pressures and policy changes but the risks are still very real.

key_quote_bn: বাংলাদেশিরা ইউরোপে সবচেয়ে বড় অভিবাসনপ্রত্যাশী হিসেবে উঠে এসেছেন।

headline_en: If people cannot go abroad with this opportunity, I will regret it: Expatriates' Welfare Minister
summary_en: Speaking at a farmer-card distribution event in Juri, Moulvibazar on 14 April 2026, Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said there is strong demand abroad for agricultural workers and that he has asked for a training centre with language courses to be opened in Juri. He also said the government is bringing home Bangladeshis stranded in the Middle East war who want to return, and promised strict action against those who send people abroad illegally.

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said on 14 April 2026 that there is considerable demand abroad for agricultural workers; he named no countries or numbers.

The minister said he has asked for arrangements to open a training centre in Juri, Moulvibazar, with cooperation from the Department of Agricultural Extension, and that a language course must be started at the training centre. This is a stated instruction; no opening date is given.
The minister said workers need Arabic for the Middle East, Japanese for Japan and English for Europe; they need not be highly proficient but must keep a minimum standard.
The minister said the government is bringing home Bangladeshi nationals who were stranded during the war in the Middle East and want to return.

The minister said strict action will be taken against manpower traders (adam byabsayi) who send people abroad by illegal means, that an inquiry into them has been ordered, and that people must also be aware about going abroad by illegal and risky means.

headline_en: Youth untraceable after torture in Libya; father-in-law and daughter-in-law arrested in trafficking case
summary_en: Limon Matubbar (22) of Madaripur paid BDT 18 lakh to Sobahan Molla and associates for a promised direct trip to Italy, left Dhaka on 11 September 2025, and was instead taken to Saudi Arabia and then Libya, where he was held and tortured. The ring extracted a further BDT 12 lakh as ransom and he has not been heard of since. His aunt filed a trafficking case against eight people on 7 April 2026; RAB arrested Sobahan's wife Tania Begum and father Salam Molla on 13 April and a court sent them to jail on 14 April.

facts.statement: Sobahan Molla and his associates promised to take Limon Matubbar (22) of Boalia village, Dudhkhali union, Madaripur Sadar directly to Italy for BDT 18 lakh; after the full amount was paid he left Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport for Italy on 11 September 2025 but was taken first to Saudi Arabia and then to Libya.
The family paid BDT 18 lakh in full before departure for the promised direct journey to Italy; later the ring collected a further BDT 12 lakh from the family as ransom, in cash and through a bank.
In Libya Limon Matubbar was held in a detention house (bondishala) and tortured; after the BDT 12 lakh ransom was paid there has been no trace of him.
On 7 April 2026 the victim's aunt Munni Akter filed a case under the human trafficking law against eight people including Sobahan Molla, his father Salam Molla and his wife Tania.

On the night of Monday 13 April 2026 members of the RAB-8 Madaripur camp arrested Tania Begum and Salam Molla at their home in Paschim Kakoir village, Shibchar upazila, Madaripur; RAB describes Sobahan Molla as a member of a human trafficking ring.

On 14 April 2026 the two arrested were handed to Madaripur Sadar Model Thana and produced in court, where Judicial Magistrate Mosa. Sabrina Tabassum ordered them sent to jail; the OC said police operations to arrest the other accused continue.
facts.source_in_article: Abul Kalam Azad, OC, Madaripur Sadar Model Thana

headline_en: Give the highest priority to ending the suffering (editorial)
summary_en: A Prothom Alo editorial drawing on a recent roundtable in Cumilla titled 'Prospects, challenges and tasks of manpower export'. It says migrants suffer from brokers, a complicated legal process, lack of coordination and one-stop service, lack of skills and weak protection abroad, and calls for a legal framework to register and regulate sub-agents, a one-stop service and unified digital platform, migration corners at district and union level, compulsory pre-departure training and stronger embassy support.

facts.statement: The editorial states that there is still no clear law or regulatory framework for the intermediaries (sub-agents, brokers) in the migration process, and calls for a legal framework to register and regulate sub-agents without delay.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing a roundtable in Cumilla

facts.statement: The editorial says that because the legal migration process is complicated and slow, many people are forced to rely on unregulated channels, resulting in fraud, extra cost, false promises and miserable conditions abroad; the Cumilla roundtable heard that a significant number of migrants are cheated this way.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo editorial, citing the roundtable

facts.statement: The editorial identifies lack of coordination between the district administration, manpower office, training centres, banks and local government, and the absence of a one-stop service, as forcing aspiring migrants to go from office to office, which gives brokers their opening; it calls for a unified digital platform or website with all migration information and services and for 'migration corners' at district and union level.

The editorial says many go abroad with no training and so get low wages and are exploited, while IT, driving or technical skills can raise income and respect; it calls for compulsory training before going abroad.

The editorial says many workers abroad face abuse, excessive workload, withheld wages or lack of legal help, and calls for an effective role by embassies, a complaint-resolution system and special protection for women workers.

key_quote_bn: অথচ এই ‘মাধ্যম’ বা ‘মধ্যস্থতাকারী’ ব্যক্তিদের জন্য এখনো সুস্পষ্ট কোনো আইন বা নিয়ন্ত্রণকাঠামো নেই।

headline_en: On making the learning of working languages compulsory in the curriculum
summary_en: A long essay (Protichinta, 5 April 2026) by Dr Ahmed Shamim of Cornell University's Language Resource Center arguing for a practical national language policy that keeps Bangla central while making 'critical' foreign languages (English, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, German and others) part of public education. For migration it cites press sources that Arabic-speaking workers can claim 20-30 percent higher wages in the Gulf, that government language training reaches only about 2,500 of roughly 1.3 million workers who left in a year, and that organised Arabic courses are lacking. Most of the essay is about US-style language resource centres and university course design.

facts.statement: The essay says workers who know Arabic can claim 20 to 30 percent higher wages in the Gulf, citing Dhaka Tribune (2024) and The Business Standard (2021, 2023).
facts.source_in_article: essay author Ahmed Shamim, citing Dhaka Tribune 2024 and The Business Standard 2021 and 2023

facts.statement: The essay says 10 lakh (1 million) workers in the Gulf lose jobs or get lower wages because they do not know Arabic, a loss it puts at USD 500 crore a year, citing Dhaka Tribune (2024) and the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre (2024).
facts.source_in_article: essay author, citing Dhaka Tribune 2024 and BHRRC 2024

facts.statement: The essay says about 13 lakh workers went abroad in a recent year (its reference is a Business Standard report on record labour migration of 13 lakh in 2023), and that of them an estimated 2,500 learned Japanese, Korean, English or Chinese at government centres.
facts.source_in_article: essay author, citing The Business Standard 2024 for the 13 lakh figure; no source given for the 2,500 estimate

facts.statement: The essay says months-long training is given for East Asian languages, but there is a lack of organised Arabic courses even though the Middle East is Bangladesh's biggest labour destination; formal government Arabic training for workers is limited and often very short, and vocational schools have no arrangement for teaching the foreign language their trade requires.

The essay argues that a construction worker who can communicate with his supervisor in Arabic is less likely to be cheated over hours, safety or wages, and that a nurse who knows German or Japanese can get training and jobs in those health systems.
facts.source_in_article: essay author (citing European Commission 2006 for the accident point)

facts.statement: The author proposes recognising languages such as English, Arabic, Chinese, Hindi-Urdu, Japanese, Korean, German, French and Russian as 'critical languages', making foreign-language learning a compulsory part of public education, setting up a National Foreign Language Resource Center under the education ministry, and running language short courses in schools, colleges and vocational institutions matched to the countries of work. These are the author's proposals, not government decisions.

key_quote_bn: তাদের মধ্যে সরকারি কেন্দ্রে জাপানি, কোরিয়ান, ইংরেজি বা চীনা শিখেছেন আনুমানিক আড়াই হাজার, যা অনুপাতে খুবই নগণ্য।

headline_en: News of another Sunamganj youth's death by starvation on that Mediterranean boat
summary_en: Mohibur Rahman (20) of Chhatak, Sunamganj is confirmed as a thirteenth Sunamganj victim of a rubber boat that left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026, lost its way for six days, ran out of fuel, food and water, and on which 22 people died of starvation. His family paid a broker BDT 13 lakh; he travelled via Saudi Arabia to Libya. Two cases against nine brokers were filed in Jagannathpur and Derai police stations on Monday night 30 March.

facts.statement: A rubber boat left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026 and lost its way in the Mediterranean; it was at sea for six days, the fuel ran out and food ran short, and 22 people on board died one after another, weakened by lack of food and clean water, most of them from Sunamganj. The others were rescued off the Greek coast on Friday 27 March 2026.

The bodies stayed on the boat for two days; when they began to smell they were thrown into the sea on the broker's instruction. News of the deaths reached relatives in Sunamganj on Saturday afternoon (28 March 2026).
Brokers call the dangerous sea journey from Libya to Greece the 'game'.

Police confirmed the identities of 12 Sunamganj people who died on the boat: six from Derai upazila, five from Jagannathpur upazila and one from Dowarabazar upazila; Mohibur Rahman of Chhatak upazila is an additional death reported by his family.

Mohibur Rahman (20) left home about four months before April 2026 to go to Greece, travelled via Saudi Arabia to Libya, and at one point messaged his family that he was suffering badly and begged to be brought home.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Sunu Mia, cousin and Bhatgaon union parishad member

facts.statement: Mohibur Rahman's family paid the broker a total of BDT 13 lakh; his poor father Nurul Amin sold land and borrowed BDT 5 lakh at moneylender's interest.

Mohibur wanted to go to Greece through Nabi Hossain of the Pagla area of Shantiganj upazila, Sunamganj, who is in Libya; Nabi Hossain's father Abdul Mannan handled all the transactions in Bangladesh, met Mohibur through masonry work and encouraged him to go to Greece.
Mohibur's father said the broker first beat his son for money, and had said he would provide a wooden boat but then put him on a plastic (rubber) boat.

Survivor Maruf Ahmad of Sunamganj, who had left Bangladesh together with Mohibur and is now in a camp in Greece after rescue, confirmed on Monday (30 March 2026) that Mohibur was the first to die on the boat, weakened by starvation, followed one by one by the others; the broker had not confirmed anything to the family.
facts.source_in_article: Maruf Ahmad, survivor, via the family

facts.statement: Following the deaths, two cases were filed against nine brokers at two police stations in Sunamganj on Monday night (30 March 2026) by the fathers of two of the dead: five accused in the Jagannathpur thana case and four in the Derai thana case; some of the accused are in Libya, Greece and Italy.

Chhatak thana OC Mohammad Mizanur Rahman said on 1 April 2026 that nobody had informed him of Mohibur's death; he saw it on social media and asked the in-charge of Jaua police outpost to look into it.

headline_en: 'My boy died crying for water, he got no water to drink'
summary_en: A report from Tiargaon village, Jagannathpur, Sunamganj on the family of Shayek Ahmad (23), one of 22 people (12 from Sunamganj) who starved to death on a small boat that left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026 and drifted for six days. His father paid local broker Azizul Islam BDT 4.5 lakh at the start and another BDT 7.5 lakh before the boat. The UNO says five from the upazila died and a list of brokers is being prepared for the police.

facts.statement: 22 people died while crossing the Mediterranean from Libya to Greece in a small boat that left Libya on 21 March 2026 and was lost at sea for six days; they died of starvation and companions put the bodies into the sea. Twelve of the dead were from Sunamganj, all young men. The Greek coast guard rescued the survivors off the Greek coast on Friday (27 March 2026).

Akhlus Mia said he first paid broker Azizul Islam BDT 4.5 lakh for his son Shayek Ahmad to go to Greece; from Libya the broker then said another BDT 7.5 lakh had to be paid before Shayek would be put on the 'game' to Greece, which the father paid by selling land and cattle.

Shayek Ahmad left home about four months before late March 2026 with several others from his area through local broker Azizul Islam and reached Libya after travelling through Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and several other countries.
The father said the broker beat his son for money before putting him on the 'game' (small boat), and that the boat had no food and no water.

Shayek's uncle, quoting a survivor's account relayed by Sohel Ahmad in Greece, said these boats are sent off with 24 hours' worth of food; food and clean water ran out after one day and, because the boat lost its way, everyone was left without food. Bodies were kept on the boat for two days before being thrown into the sea.
facts.source_in_article: Angur Mia, uncle, quoting Sohel Ahmad

facts.statement: Shayek could not board on the first attempt because he injured his leg while getting into the boat; he was then put on the 21 March 2026 'game'.

The family learned of the death on Saturday (28 March 2026) when Sohel Ahmad, a young man from the same area living in Greece, phoned after visiting the camp where the rescued survivors were held and asking them about Shayek.

Jagannathpur UNO Mohammad Barkatullah said five people from the upazila died on the Libya-Greece crossing, that he was visiting all their homes, and that a list of brokers was being made to hand to the police for action.
Raniganj union parishad chairman Sheikh Sadrul Islam said two young men from his union alone died on the boat.
facts.source_in_article: Sheikh Sadrul Islam, UP chairman, Raniganj

headline_en: Middle East war will affect remittances: Expatriates' Welfare Minister
summary_en: On Sunday 8 March 2026 in Sylhet, Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the ongoing war in the Middle East will have some effect on remittances. He said the first task is to keep expatriates there safe with logistic support, that bringing them home is being kept in mind, and that a monitoring cell has been formed. He said efforts to reopen closed labour markets are not possible in the Middle East because of the war, so the government is trying to the east.

facts.statement: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the government's first task is to keep Bangladeshi expatriates in the Middle East on the safe side and give them logistic support; depending on how the war situation develops, bringing them home is also being kept in mind, and treatment will be arranged for anyone who is injured.

A monitoring cell has been formed with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the civil aviation ministry, all embassies and the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare on the safety of expatriates during the Middle East war; the minister said the situation is monitored daily. No contact number is given.

The minister said efforts are under way to reopen labour markets that have closed to Bangladesh, but this is not possible in the Middle East now because of the war, so the government is trying towards the east; progress is slow because of Ramadan and the war and he hoped it would pick up from the following month. No countries are named.

The minister said it is natural that the Middle East war will have some effect on remittances, and that the government has taken various initiatives for remitters which would become visible within some days; he gave no details.
